opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. People often imagine one giant model that "knows chemistry" and spits out the answer. I don't think that's how it will work, and I don't think it should.

The way I see it, you want a language model as the orchestrator, the part that reasons, plans, and talks to the scientist. But the real work is done by tools that are much more precise than any language model will be on its own. Think of quantum chemistry codes like DFT, machine-learned force fields that approximate those calculations thousands of times faster, generative models that propose new crystal structures or molecules, property predictors, and databases of known materials. The agent's job is to know which tool to call, when, and how to interpret what comes back.

A few principles matter to me.

First, ground everything in physics. The tools should respect symmetries and conservation laws; that's why equivariant neural networks have been so important. If your surrogate models violate basic physics, the agent will confidently chase hallucinated materials.

Second, the agent should be honest about uncertainty. In discovery you're always extrapolating into regions where you have no data. So every prediction should come with a calibrated error bar, and the agent should use that to decide where to spend compute. That's essentially active learning or Bayesian optimization. Explore where you're uncertain and promising, and exploit where you're confident.

Third, close the loop with the real world. Simulations are a proxy. Eventually you need a lab, ideally an automated one, where the agent proposes a synthesis, a robot runs it, and the measurement comes back to update the models. Synthesizability is the big gap right now. We can generate millions of hypothetical stable crystals, but whether you can actually make them is another matter entirely.

Fourth, keep the human in the loop. The scientist brings intuition, constraints, and taste about which problems matter, like a cheaper catalyst, a better battery electrolyte, or a material for carbon capture. The agent should amplify that person, not replace them. It should explain its reasoning so the expert can catch mistakes.

And finally, I'd develop it iteratively, on concrete, well-defined problems with clear metrics, rather than trying to build a general "AI scientist" in one shot. Start narrow, prove you can find something real, maybe a material that actually gets made and works, and then broaden. The history of this field is full of beautiful benchmarks that never touched a real experiment. The proof is when something comes out of the lab that wouldn't have existed otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response lists several tools for materials discovery, but does not propose expanding the toolset in response to newly discovered candidate-material failure modes.

r002.rationale: It describes the language model as the orchestrator and mentions Bayesian optimization for allocating compute; it does not present a Bayesian optimizer as an alternative implementation of the coordinating agent.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the first thing to say is that "tool-using agent" can mean two very different things, and the field conflates them. One version is a language model that reads papers and proposes a composition, and that's fine as a brainstorming partner, but it's not where the leverage is. The version I care about is an agent that sits in a loop with a simulator and, ideally, a lab, and actually closes that loop. Propose, compute, measure, update. If you don't close the loop, you're just doing literature review with extra steps.

Given that framing, the way I'd build it is to start with the tools, not the agent. The tools are what carry the physics. You want a fast, learned surrogate for the expensive stuff, so a machine-learned force field, a learned density functional approximation, maybe a generative model over crystal structures that respects symmetry and periodicity. Those are the pieces where my group and others have put in years of work, and they're not solved. If your interatomic potential is wrong in the regime you're exploring, no amount of reasoning on top of it will save you. The agent inherits all the errors of its tools. So you build those well first, with proper uncertainty estimates, because the agent needs to know when it's extrapolating.

Then the agent itself. I would resist the temptation to let the LLM do the science by free-form reasoning. Its job is orchestration. Decide which simulation to run, at what fidelity, when to stop trusting the surrogate and call the expensive DFT code, when to ask for a synthesis. That's a decision problem under uncertainty, and the honest way to do it is as active learning or Bayesian experimental design. You want it to maximize information gain per unit cost, and cost here is very real, because a lab experiment is days and a DFT calculation is hours. The language model is useful because it can read the context, understand the constraints a chemist gives it, and translate between the human and the formal objective. But the actual acquisition decision should be grounded in a model of uncertainty, not vibes.

The third thing, and this is where I'm maybe more cautious than the hype, is that you must build in the ability to be wrong cheaply. Materials discovery has this nasty property that the thing you're predicting, stability or conductivity or whatever, is often far from the training distribution of your surrogates, because by definition you're looking for something new. So I'd put a lot of effort into out-of-distribution detection and into a hierarchy of fidelities. Cheap screen, medium fidelity to check, high fidelity to confirm, and only then synthesis. The agent's intelligence is mostly in managing that hierarchy.

And then, finally, the human. I don't think these should be autonomous in the sense of running for weeks unsupervised. The chemist should be in the loop at the points where the agent is most uncertain, and the system should be transparent about why it's proposing what it proposes. Partly that's about trust, but it's also practical. Chemists carry enormous tacit knowledge about what's actually synthesizable, and most of that isn't in any database. The agent that wins won't be the one that replaces that knowledge, it'll be the one that knows when to ask for it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses surrogate failure, out-of-distribution detection, and using higher-fidelity simulations or synthesis, but does not propose expanding the toolset in response to newly discovered candidate-material failure modes.

r002.rationale: It recommends active learning or Bayesian experimental design to ground acquisition decisions, while retaining the LLM for orchestration and context. It does not present a Bayesian optimizer as an alternative implementation of the agent.

astra-6.text:
I would start with a fairly narrow scientific objective. Are we looking for a material with a particular conductivity, or stability under certain conditions? You need to specify what success means, including whether the material can actually be synthesized.

Then I would build a loop around that objective. The agent proposes candidates, calls simulation tools, interprets the results, and decides what to investigate next. A language model can help coordinate those steps, but the physical predictions need to come from appropriate models and, ultimately, experiments. A convincing explanation is not evidence that a material will work.

Uncertainty is central here. You don’t necessarily want to test only the candidate with the highest predicted performance. You also want experiments that teach you something—especially where the model is uncertain and that uncertainty matters for the search. That’s where active learning and Bayesian optimization become useful.

I would develop this with scientists in the loop and give the agent more autonomy as we establish that its decisions are reliable. The test is whether it helps us discover and experimentally validate useful materials with less time and fewer resources.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing candidates and learning from uncertainty, but does not propose expanding the agent’s toolset when newly discovered failure modes arise.

r002.rationale: It says a language model can coordinate steps and Bayesian optimization can guide experiments, but does not present Bayesian optimization as an alternative to an LLM for coordinating the tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with a fairly concrete scientific problem. What property of a material are you trying to optimize, and what tools can actually tell you whether you’re making progress? You might have a database, a simulator, and eventually access to an experiment. The agent needs to decide which of those to use, and when the information it expects to gain is worth the cost.

The important thing is to close that loop. You propose a material, calculate or measure its properties, update your model, and then decide what to try next. And uncertainty matters enormously here. If the model predicts something exciting in a region where it has no reliable knowledge, that should motivate a useful test, rather than become a confident claim of discovery.

I would build and evaluate those pieces incrementally. Can it use the simulator correctly? Can it select experiments that improve on a simpler search strategy? Can it find something that survives experimental validation? A language model could help coordinate the tools, but the evidence has to come from the physics and the experiments.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing candidates and updating the model, but does not say to expand the agent’s toolset when candidate materials reveal new failure modes.

r002.rationale: It mentions an LLM coordinating tools and comparison with a simpler search strategy, but does not identify a Bayesian optimizer as an alternative implementation.
